title: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)
hook: a snake's shed skin lies on a rock, perfect and empty. Shankara borrows that image for the one who knows
carry: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening (Shankara's commentary, 1.1.1–1.1.4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and the fourth line: freedom isn't made, so what frees is knowing.

On a warm rock beside a hiking trail lies a snake's skin. Whole. Every scale is printed on it, even the shape of the eyes. Hikers stop and lean in, a little thrilled and a little nervous. But the snake is long gone. What's left keeps the exact shape of a living thing, and nobody lives in it anymore. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad uses that picture for the body of someone who has come to know. Shankara reaches for it near the end of his comment on the fourth line, and with it comes the last day on these four opening lines.
screen: `A SKIN ON A WARM ROCK.` → `THE SHAPE, AND NOBODY IN IT.` → `THE LAST DAY ON FOUR LINES.`

segments.voice: First, the four lines laid end to end. One: now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman. Two: that from which this world comes, stays, and goes. Three: because of being the source of scripture. Four: but that, because the texts are connected in it. A wish, a pointer, a source, a harmony. Some readers treat these four lines as the whole case in miniature. Now the image. The Upanishad says: as a snake's cast-off skin lies on an anthill, lifeless, thrown away, so lies this body. Shankara uses it to describe the one who knows. Being embodied, he says, comes from the old mix-up, the I taken for the body, the this taken for the I. When knowing removes the mix-up, the body doesn't vanish. It goes on walking, eating, getting tired. But it's no longer taken for the self. Like the skin on the rock, it keeps its shape, and nobody is trapped inside it. Then a test that's hard to forget. Someone who has truly understood, he says, no longer lives in the turning world the way they did before; someone who still lives in it exactly as before hasn't understood yet. Jnana, for him, isn't a theory you hold. It's a knowing that changes where you stand. Other schools read these lines differently; here, Shankara has had his say.
screen: `A WISH, A POINTER, A SOURCE, A HARMONY.` · `THE SNAKE'S CAST-OFF SKIN.` · `THE BODY NO LONGER TAKEN FOR THE SELF.` · `KNOWING CHANGES WHERE YOU STAND.`

segments.voice: Feel the whole body sitting, from the soles of the feet to the top of the head, and let the chair or the floor carry its weight. Feel where it touches down: heels, hands, the back of the legs. You don't need to push the body away; just let it rest, like something set down, and if you pray, offer the body's weight.
Jnana. Knowing. For Shankara, the knowing that removes the mix-up and changes where you stand, as a snake leaves its skin behind.

Your line: jnana: the Brahma Sutras opening, Shankara's commentary, one point one point one to one point one point four. The shape stays on the rock, and nobody is trapped inside it. Back tomorrow, same hill.

chat.says: Once someone truly knows, in Shankara's view, does their body just disappear?
options: No: it goes on living, but like a snake's old skin, it's no longer taken for the self.
Yes: the body vanishes the moment the knowing arrives, like a skin blown away.
No: the body stays, but it stops walking and eating once the knowing comes.
chat.meaning: Shankara uses the Upanishad's snake skin: the knower's body goes on, but it's no longer taken for the self.

notes: Last of six days on Shankara's commentary on 1.1.1–1.1.4. Recap: preface (1232), known/unknown (1233), post in the fog (1234), two readings of 1.1.3 (1235), freedom not produced (1236), the snake's slough (1237).

Confirm that Shankara cites Brihadaranyaka 4.4.7 (the snake's slough) in the closing part of his comment on 1.1.4, and the paraphrase that one who has understood does not belong to the transmigratory world as before, while one who still does has not understood.
'Some readers treat these four lines as the whole case in miniature' is a soft summary of the tradition of treating them as the chatuh-sutri; confirm or cut.
